messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi had been a chef in the United States for several years, but the event that haunted him belonged to the road he fled as a refugee in South Asia, where a convoy was hit and the noise of the impact, the shouting, and the sight of people with torn, bleeding skin had never really left him. In the aftermath, he had been the one moving between frightened bodies, and he still carried the sense that he had not done enough to stop what happened or help the people who died. When he tried to describe it later, the story broke apart; he could point to fragments, but the frightening moment itself seemed to sit in him without words. At other times he could picture it with a strange blankness, as if it had happened to someone else, and then the numbness would crack into overwhelming grief. Those memories fed the beliefs he had come to live with: that he would never forgive himself for not doing more, that he should feel guilty for surviving when others did not, and that the experience had permanently changed him for the worse.

In the years since, those appraisals began shaping everything else. Ravi became extremely vigilant, especially in public places and at work, where he watched the door, the windows, and the people around him while he chopped vegetables or moved between the stove and the service line. He always identified escape routes before he could feel comfortable anywhere, and open or exposed spaces made him feel unprotected, so he chose seats near walls, kept to the edge of rooms, and avoided broad parking lots or plazas whenever he could. Part of that was a practical response to how easily reminders caught him off guard: ambulances slicing past with sirens, a colleague casually discussing a car accident, or the flash of a wound on a customer or coworker could turn his attention rigid and pull him back into the old fear. But those same reminders also made his mind race with the belief that danger could return without warning and that he would be helpless in the moment. When he noticed those signs, he became more guarded, more watchful, and more intent on finding a way out before he let himself settle.

Ravi also tried to manage the fear in ways that made immediate sense to him but kept the pattern going. In places where he felt threatened, he became overly compliant, smiling too quickly, agreeing too readily, and keeping his voice soft so no one would challenge him. Around police or military uniforms, or even the sight of weapons, he pulled back and tried to disappear into the background. He had come to believe that if he stayed small, stayed agreeable, and avoided anything that looked like force, he might reduce the chance of being trapped again. Yet those choices only deepened his sense that he was no longer the man he had been. The more he arranged his life around danger, the more he felt his character had been altered, and that conviction pushed his guilt harder: he blamed himself for failing before and now blamed himself for living in fear. At work, he began turning down opportunities that would require him to step into the dining room during crowded events or to assist in outdoor catering jobs in open spaces, which affected his standing with his employer and left him increasingly isolated.

The same efforts also changed the way his memories came back. When he was scanning exits, avoiding uniforms, or shrinking himself to keep others calm, the event returned in pieces that were harder to place into a coherent story. He could see flashes of injuries, hear an ambulance in the distance, or feel the old helplessness, but the more he pushed himself to stay safe, the more the memory seemed to retreat into wordless fragments and numb, stranger-like scenes. Even brief reminders now seemed potent because they had become linked to his own rules for safety and blame. Seeing an ambulance outside the restaurant, hearing coworkers mention a crash, or noticing a customer’s bandaged arm did not only jar him; they confirmed, in his mind, that danger was still nearby and that his failure and survival still defined him. That belief kept his concentration poor, his body tense, and his attention constantly scanning for the next threat.

By the time he sought help, Ravi was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of what frightened him. He had noticed that the world was shrinking around his routines at work and in daily life, and that his fear of ambulances, accident talk, visible wounds, uniforms, and open spaces was making him more isolated and less able to concentrate on the job he depended on. What brought him in was the sense that the cycle was tightening and that he could no longer tell whether he was protecting himself or living as if the danger had already taken over. He was afraid that if he kept going this way, he would lose the rest of his confidence and maybe his work, but he also hoped that if he could finally make sense of the memories and the guilt, he might stop living every day as though he were still on that road.
